definition.text: The study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live in soil.

facts.text: Soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon, covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface.
Soil organisms include bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, earthworms and arthropods, along with some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs.
Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity.
By decomposing organic matter, soil organisms release nutrients for plants and strongly shape soil fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage.
Soil life powers nutrient cycles: without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no humus and no nutrients available to plants.
Nutrients held in the bodies of soil organisms are kept from leaching away, nitrogen and phosphorus in particular.
Microbial exudates help maintain soil structure, and earthworms mix the soil through bioturbation.
It is a relatively new science with much still unknown; the discovery of glomalin in 1996 showed that basic questions about soil biogeochemical cycles remained open.

title: Soil bacteria

definition.text: The single-celled prokaryotic organisms of the soil, its most numerous inhabitants.

facts.text: A 'teaspoon' of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria, and up to 10 billion culturable cells live in each gram of soil in and around plant roots.
They live in soil water, including the moisture film around particles, where some swim with flagella, and multiply fast by binary fission when conditions suit.
Most beneficial soil bacteria are aerobic and most active in moist but unsaturated soil of neutral pH with plenty of food; anaerobic bacteria tend to putrefy dead organic matter.
Away from roots, most bulk-soil bacteria rest as drought-resistant colonies in a polysaccharide matrix coated with clay platelets, until root exudates or earthworm mucus reach them.
Hostile conditions send them dormant: Gram-positive Bacillus and Clostridium form spores, and Gram-negative bacteria enter a nonculturable resting stage.
Bacteria carry out key steps of the nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation, nitrification by chemolithotrophs such as Nitrosomonas, and denitrification in oxygen-free conditions.
Their biochemistry is versatile: Pseudomonas can metabolize a wide range of chemicals, while Nitrobacter gets its energy only by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate.
Soil archaea, also prokaryotes, are still poorly known but may matter in nitrification and methanogenesis; some bacteria colonize minerals and speed their weathering.

title: Soil fungi

definition.text: The yeasts, moulds and other fungi of the soil, which lack chlorophyll and spread through the soil as threads called mycelium, feeding on organic matter.

facts.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal hyphae.
Fungi may be outnumbered by bacteria in cell counts but can contribute greater biomass and respiration in some soils.
As chemo-heterotrophs they need organic substrates for carbon; their mycelium breaks fresh remains down into humus and carbon dioxide.
For humus formation the key fungi are saprotrophs, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use.
Dead matter is colonised by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and lignin.
Many are parasites that cause plant disease, while others are beneficial symbionts such as mycorrhizae; fungi also aid aggregation and feed larger soil organisms.
Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need.
Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

title: Soil ecosystem engineers

definition.text: Species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat; in soil, chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, and fungi.

facts.text: They are defined by their ability to modify resources for other organisms, not by being eaten, which sets them apart from keystone species.
Allogenic engineers change materials mechanically, as burrowers do; autogenic engineers create habitat with their own bodies, as Sphagnum moss builds peatlands.
Earthworms, ants and termites mix the soil as they burrow, strongly affecting soil formation and organic matter dynamics while building granular structure.
Ant and termite nests change the soil chemically and physically, enriching it in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and mixing particles from different depths.
Burrowing mammals such as moles, gophers and prairie dogs turn soil, spread mycorrhizal fungi and open underground corridors used by arthropods, birds, small mammals and reptiles.
Fungi are engineers too: by linking distant patches and moving nutrients between them, even redistributing carbon between trees, they control nutrient cycles.
Where earthworm activity is poor, enchytraeids take on the role, digging galleries in which they deposit their faeces.
Earthworms are particularly sensitive to many contaminants, and the loss of such engineers brings dramatic changes in humus forms.

contested_note: Some ecologists treat the term as a buzzword, arguing that it implies intent or that every species would qualify.

definition.text: The study of how soil organisms interact with one another and with their environment.

facts.text: This branch of ecology is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, soil aggregate formation and soil biodiversity.
Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem.
Soil is a heterogeneous mix of minerals and organic matter whose variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms.
Moisture is a major limiting factor: soil organisms constantly face dehydration, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting.
Soil temperature fluctuates less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, mineralization and decomposition.
Most soil organisms are aerobic: microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move about.
Patchy soil properties across the landscape, and changes between horizons, make soil communities patchy and stratified with depth.
Soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models of soil processes, partly from assuming that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

definition.text: Small sites in soil, rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients, where microorganisms are concentrated.

facts.text: Examples are the rhizosphere and the detritusphere, where organic matter accumulates.
There, decaying root litter and root exudates regulate the supply of carbon and nitrogen and so steer microbial processes.
Root tips are hotspots of cellulase and chitinase activity.
The spatial separation of microbes, shaped by labile carbon, temperature and moisture, affects how they interact and how the soil ecosystem functions.

title: Global patterns of soil biodiversity

definition.text: The unsettled question of how life in soil is distributed over the globe and whether it follows the same drivers as life above ground.

facts.text: A survey of 17,516 18S rRNA gene sequences from 20 phyla of soil animals suggested that below-ground animal diversity may be inversely related to above-ground diversity.
Soil biodiversity lacks the clear latitudinal gradients of plants; in 2007 salinity, not temperature or pH, was found to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity.
A 2014 global study found fungal richness unrelated to plant diversity and better explained by climate, then soil and spatial factors.
Some studies find that losing soil organisms reduces many ecosystem functions; others find above-ground plant diversity a better predictor of multifunctionality.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether soil biodiversity mirrors above-ground diversity and how strongly it drives ecosystem functioning.

definition.text: The relationship between soil and the variety of life, and the aspects of soil that can be managed with that variety in mind.

facts.text: Soil is a habitat chiefly for microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also for microfauna (protozoa, nematodes), mesofauna (microarthropods, enchytraeids) and macrofauna (earthworms, termites, millipedes).
The primary role of soil biota is to recycle organic matter that comes from the above-ground, plant-based food web.
In turn, biological activity is a primary factor in the physical and chemical formation of soil.
Natural and agricultural vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales.
Microbial exudates are now accepted as dominating the aggregation of soil particles and the protection of carbon from further breakdown.
The organisms beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep.
Soil health depends on soil biodiversity and can be improved by keeping living covers on the soil and adding carbon-containing amendments.
Management matters: crop rotation, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs correlate with higher soil diversity.

definition.text: Soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinisation, sodicity, structure decline and erosion, many of them driven by how soil is managed.

facts.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike.
Acidification cuts the numbers of most macrofauna, earthworms included, harms rhizobium survival and may slow decomposition and nitrogen fixation.
At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less.
Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and decomposing organic matter more slowly.
Erosion strips topsoil, organic matter and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat to soil biodiversity.
Constant tillage redistributes soil organic matter, degrading structure and altering populations of organisms such as earthworms.
Chloride from potassium chloride fertilizer raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, nitrifiers included.

title: Measuring soil biodiversity

definition.text: Ways of counting and identifying soil organisms, increasingly by extracting DNA directly from the soil.

facts.text: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so the diversity of soil life is hard to measure.
Next-generation sequencing and DNA extracted directly from the soil matrix are opening soil diversity to study.
Omics approaches such as metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and proteomics are advancing fast for microbes; metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints.
A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

notes: Facts also draw on Soil ecology § Soil microbes and § Microfauna, and Soil conservation.

definition.text: The study of the microorganisms in soil, what they do and how they affect soil properties.

facts.text: Soil microorganisms are grouped as bacteria (including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes), archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and protozoa.
The first cyanobacteria, which arose two to four billion years ago, fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil.
Microbial diversity in soil depends on pH, texture, organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals.
In 2011 more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species were detected on sugar beet roots.
Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses.
A more diverse soil microbiome generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields.
Soil microbes communicate through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular polysaccharides, and exchange metabolites that support one another's growth.
Cover crops raise soil microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

title: Soil actinomycetes

definition.text: Soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia.

facts.text: They decompose the organic matter of dead organisms so plants can take it up anew, and build humus by breaking down cellulose, lignin and arthropod chitin.
Fungi play a similar role, but actinomycetota are much smaller and likely fill a different niche; the order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi.

The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups and includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera; Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils.
Some, such as Frankia, live symbiotically with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars.
Their volatile metabolites give healthy soil its sweet, earthy smell.
They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi.
They yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, and agricultural compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.
They break large lignin molecules into smaller pieces; lignin is hard for most organisms to break down and often shields cellulose from decomposition.

definition.text: Photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon from light.

facts.text: Needing light, they are spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach, not far below the surface.
Below the surface they can live given steady temperature and moisture, feeding heterotrophically on easy carbon sources such as glucose.
Soil algae divide into green Chlorophyceae and golden-brown diatoms, coloured by the carotenoid fucoxanthin.
Chlorella vulgaris has been shown to promote plant growth together with rhizosphere bacteria.

definition.text: Single-celled eukaryotes of the soil, grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates.

facts.text: Most eat bacteria; others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of humus.
Flagellates are the smallest; heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million per gram of soil.
Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films, while testate amoebae shelter in shells against drying and serve as indicators of past climates.
Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

title: Soil microbial loop

definition.text: The pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web; in soil it concerns soil carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and nematodes eat root-fed bacteria.

facts.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles; 'microbial food web' is now often used instead.
Roots exploring new soil prime quiescent bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat, freeing mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb.
Predation by amoebae and free-living nematodes raises the mineralization rate, which in turn stimulates root growth; Clarholm's hypothesis of this loop is hard to verify experimentally.
Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial biomass in a form plants can use.

The microbial carbon pump model has plants add carbon through root exudates and litter; microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in the stable pool as dead microbial biomass (necromass).

Microbes transform plant carbon outside the cell with extracellular enzymes and inside it through biomass turnover; the balance of CO2-releasing and carbon-building pathways sets net carbon retention.
Fresh plant carbon can prime microbes to decompose existing soil organic carbon faster than models expect.
Most of the soil microbiome is uncultivated, which leaves its contribution to soil carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

notes: Extended in gap-fill with the crawled Microbial loop page (§ In land ecosystems). Also on Soil microbiology, Soil animals and Soil formation.

definition.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities.

facts.text: Phage richness varies with season, soil moisture, location and plant growth, and rises with bacterial abundance.
Soil phages may be lytic, killing the host to release virions, lysogenic, joining the host genome, or chronic, releasing virions without killing it.
By killing hosts, lytic phages affect bacterial cycling of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus; phages are also a major agent of horizontal gene transfer.
Phages can open plants to disease: phage ΦGP100 kills Pseudomonas fluorescens, which produces antifungals.

definition.text: Soil microorganisms whose single cells join into syncytia (slime molds, which are eukaryotes) or swarms (myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes).

facts.text: These collective organisms glide in a coordinated way when foraging, a behaviour still largely unexplored.
Both groups form spores in fruiting bodies, often iridescent and conspicuous.
Slime molds make complex nutritional decisions with no coordination centre, as a single vast multinucleate cell.

title: Agricultural use of soil microbes

definition.text: Using and managing soil microorganisms to make nutrients available to crops, spur their growth and protect them from disease.

facts.text: Healthy soil life can supply nutrients such as nitrogen and protect crops against pests and diseases while reducing the need for water and other inputs.
Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots.
Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market.
Long-marketed examples are Trichoderma fungi that suppress pathogenic fungi and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis.
Many strains that looked promising in the lab fail in the field because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects.
Introduced populations can fade, as Bacillus subtilis does for lack of a defensible niche; using several collaborating strains helps.
Rules demanding safety evidence have led many products to call themselves 'biostimulants' rather than 'biopesticides'.
Excess fertilizer can suppress mycorrhizae, phosphorus in particular above a threshold, and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors.

definition.text: The study of animals that live wholly or partly in the soil, also called pedozoology.

facts.text: Mercury Ghilarov developed the field in Russia in the 1940s.
Ghilarov noted that the smaller soil organisms are, the more numerous they are, and suggested soil may have been the transitional environment between aquatic and terrestrial life.
The term was apparently first used in English at a 1955 conference of soil zoologists at the University of Nottingham.
Studying interactions among soil animals can help farmers cut chemical use through integrated pest management.

title: Soil animals

definition.text: The animals that live in soil for their whole life or at least as larvae; about 30% of arthropods live in soil.

facts.text: Soil shelters animals from swings in temperature and moisture and from predators, supplies food all year and offers a safe place to lay eggs.
By increasing body size, soil fauna are classed as microfauna (20 μm to 200 μm), mesofauna (200 μm to 2 mm), macrofauna (2 mm to 2 cm) and megafauna (more than 2 cm).
Size sets an animal's place in the soil food web: bigger species eat smaller ones or modify their environment.
Many are adapted to life underground: smaller, blind, unpigmented, legless or short-legged, and often reproducing asexually.
They are tightly linked with microbes, which feed them and help digest tough compounds, while the animals' guts, faeces and cavities house microbes, disperse them and regulate their numbers.
Soil may have been a crucible for the evolution of land invertebrates, a step between aquatic and aerial life.
Animals must be extracted, expelled, trapped or hand-sorted and named by specialists, which slowed soil zoology; DNA barcoding now yields full species lists, cryptic species included.
Whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated; organic fertilizers raised soil fauna abundance while mineral fertilizers did not.

contested_note: Sources say it is still debated whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals.
notes: Size class limits differ on Soil biology § Overview; see the conflicts on Soil mesofauna.

title: Soil microfauna

definition.text: The smallest soil animals, 20 μm to 200 μm in size: protozoa and tiny multicellular animals such as nematodes, rotifers and tardigrades.

facts.text: They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots, eating microbes or other microfauna.
Grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and microfauna excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use.
Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying, but cryptobiotic stages such as cysts, dauer larvae and tardigrade tuns wait out bad times and revive within a few hours.
Unlike most soil invertebrates they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.
Nematodes and protozoa, abundant in soil, shape rhizosphere functions; root-feeding nematodes alter the soil's organic carbon.
Protozoa release phosphorus and nitrogen by dissolving organic material, and their grazing keeps bacterial populations decomposing efficiently, improving fertility.
Selective grazing changes the diversity of rhizosphere microbes and speeds their turnover.

notes: Soil biology § Overview lumps 'microfauna and microflora' at 1 to 100 micrometres (S:16c14cc1c375), a different grouping that includes microbes, so it is not listed as a conflict. Raised to Major in the discovery pass with facts from the Microfauna page; its population figure (S:93298c3e9186) is garbled in the source (per g with a 0.1 g gloss) and was not used.

definition.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 0.2 mm and 2 mm, chiefly microarthropods such as mites and springtails, and potworms (enchytraeids).

facts.text: They feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals, and their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the carbon cycle.
Microarthropods cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction; enchytraeids instead dig galleries.
By eating fungal hyphae and spores they help regulate fungal communities, mycorrhizal fungi included, both spreading and severing them.
Springtails, with high reproductive rates and large populations, are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, making them pivotal in soil food webs.
They eat and break down the faeces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts.
Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality.
Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, land use change and agricultural intensification.

conflicts.text: Mesofauna: size range 100 micrometres to 2 mm.
conflicts.note: Soil biology § Overview puts the lower limit at 100 μm; Soil animals puts it at 200 μm (0.2 mm).

conflicts.text: Mesofauna are soil animals from 0.1 to 2 millimeters in length.
conflicts.note: Soil respiration § Soil animals also puts the lower limit at 0.1 mm, against 0.2 mm on Soil animals.

definition.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm, such as earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails.

facts.text: Earthworms, termites, ants, some millipedes and some insect larvae make pore spaces and so change soil structure.
Diets differ: millipedes, woodlice and some earthworms eat leaf litter, lower termites eat wood, endogeic earthworms and higher termites eat humus, and centipedes and spiders hunt prey.
Shredding plant remains and waking dormant bacteria in the soil they swallow speeds decomposition: the 'Sleeping Beauty' paradigm, with the earthworm as 'Prince Charming'.
Saprophagous macrofauna need enzymes from gut microbes to digest wood or soil organic matter; in lower termites, symbiotic flagellates help digest lignocellulose.
Food ground in earthworm gizzards or chewed by termites leaves pasty faeces that harden into stable earthworm casts and termite mounds.
Abundant in fertile soils, they are typical of mull humus, with many trophic niches and more complex food webs.
Needing much calcium and nitrogen, they depend on plants with fast-decaying litter, and by speeding nutrient cycling they favour such plants: a positive above- and below-ground feedback.

title: Soil megafauna

definition.text: Soil animals over 2 cm long, mostly burrowing vertebrates, that dig nests and galleries and throw earth up into mounds.

facts.text: They include fossorial mammals such as moles, pocket gophers, voles and badgers, plus burrowing birds, reptiles, amphibians, large earthworms and big arthropods; they are most common in arid areas.
Most dig without eating soil, but stirring the horizons improves nutrient availability, infiltration, aeration, mycorrhizal inoculation and seed germination.
Burrows create nutrient-rich patches and raise porosity and infiltration, reducing runoff on slopes.
Often treated as pests, their loss from whole landscapes has been called an ecological catastrophe, especially in dry lands where they are keystone species for soil health.

notes: Also draws on Soil biology § Vertebrates.

title: Soil food web

definition.text: The community of organisms living all or part of their lives in the soil, viewed as the network of feeding links that passes energy among them.

facts.text: Unlike a food chain, which follows one linear energy pathway, a food web shows all the potential pathways.
Plants are the producers, using sunlight to make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals; their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground.
Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to nematodes and microarthropods, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates.
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients; all soil organic matter is processed through the web as in a digestive system.
It keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and raises infiltration.
Soil organisms also prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground.
Once thought simple, soil food webs proved to have common omnivory and long, complex chains that still resist drying, freezing and fumigation.
Litter transformers, mutualists and ecosystem engineers strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

title: Types of soil food webs
article: Soil food web#Types of food webs

definition.text: The three ways of drawing a food web: topological webs, flow webs and interaction webs.

facts.text: Topological webs, the earliest kind, map which organisms eat which without numbers; the first, in 1912, covered predators and parasites of the cotton boll weevil.
How many species are lumped into functional groups varies by author, which hampers standardized comparisons.
Interaction webs show how one group influences another: each link has a positive effect on the consumer and a negative one on the resource, and these can cause indirect effects.
Community matrix models describe every link with differential equations, using Lotka–Volterra equations and data on biomass and feeding rate to calculate interaction strengths.

title: Soil flow webs

definition.text: Food webs that add numbers to the feeding links, tracing how much carbon or other nutrients move from producers to consumers.

facts.text: Hunt et al. (1987) published the first soil flow web, for the shortgrass prairie of Colorado, estimating nitrogen transfer and mineralization rates for a range of soil organisms.
Building one starts from a topological web; each functional group's biomass is then calculated, usually in kg carbon/hectare, assuming populations are at equilibrium to derive feeding rates.
Flow webs revealed three main energy channels: the bacterial and fungal channels carry the largest flow, the root-herbivory channel much less.
Bacteria and fungi are now widely recognized as critical to decomposing carbon and nitrogen in both cycles.

title: Bottom-up control in soil food webs

definition.text: Control of a food web from its base, where the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels.

facts.text: Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and their resources are evidence of bottom-up control.
On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity.
More productivity means more leaf litter, more bacteria and fungi, more nematodes that eat them and more mites and predatory nematodes: the whole web swells.

distinct_from: Top-down control in soil food webs

title: Top-down control in soil food webs

definition.text: Control of a food web from above, where consumers at higher levels set the abundance, diversity or biomass of lower levels.

facts.text: In a trophic cascade, predators affect organisms at least two links down; whether cascades matter on land is actively debated, and in soil they occur in bacterial and fungal channels but may be infrequent.
Omnivory, dormancy and the spatial separation of predator and prey all damp top-down effects in soil.
Soil food webs are donor controlled: decomposers cannot change how fast litter falls, which limits top-down effects.
Added predators or parasites can still matter: an entomopathogenic nematode that kills root-eating ghost moth caterpillars protected bush lupine, the principle behind biological control.

contested_note: The importance of trophic cascades and top-down control on land, and whether cascades occur in soil, is actively debated.

title: Stability of soil food webs
article: Soil food web#Stability of food webs

definition.text: How well soil food webs resist and recover from disturbance, and why their complexity seems to help.

facts.text: May's models, with randomly linked community matrices, predicted that complexity destabilizes food webs, and soil webs were long thought simple; the random matrices drew much criticism.
Soil food webs did not fit those predictions: long, complex, omnivorous chains resisted drying, freezing and fumigation.
Many weak interactions, donor control, the buffering of soil structure and dormancy in organisms such as bacteria all promote stability.
Nitrogen-containing fertilizers reduce stability because they acidify soil.

title: Soil fauna extraction methods

definition.text: Techniques for separating organisms from soil samples so they can be counted and identified.

facts.text: Samples are often taken with a metal core; large animals such as earthworms are picked out by hand, which is impossible for nematodes and small arthropods.
A dry Berlese funnel drives microarthropods down away from light and heat into a collecting vial; a wet Baermann funnel collects nematodes, which sink because they cannot swim.
Microbes are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

title: External rumen
article: Soil food web#Interactions not included in food webs

definition.text: A partnership in which litter-eating animals such as isopods let microbes enrich their faecal pellets outside the body, then eat the pellets again.

facts.text: Isopods and other litter transformers excrete pellets that are moister and richer in nutrients than the surrounding soil, which bacteria and fungi then colonise.
On nutrient-poor litter the microbes enrich the food, and isopods kept from eating their own faeces can die.
Fungi play a similar role for wood-eaters, enriching nutritionally scarce dead wood so xylophages can develop and speed wood decay.
Such mutualisms and habitat changes are not captured by standard food webs, which emphasise competition and predation.

title: Soil respiration

definition.text: The production of carbon dioxide by respiring roots, rhizosphere microbes and soil fauna below ground.

facts.text: It is a key ecosystem process that returns soil carbon to the air as CO2: carbon fixed by photosynthesis is respired by roots or by the heterotrophs that consume plant material.
Temperature, moisture, nutrient content and oxygen make rates vary enormously; oxygen gradients in aggregates create anoxic microsites where anaerobic metabolism dominates.
Researchers estimate that soil respiration releases 77 Pg of carbon a year, more than human sources such as fossil fuel burning.
Global soils hold up to 3150 Pg of carbon, more than four times the atmosphere, so a small change in soil respiration can upset the balance of atmospheric CO2.
Litter decomposition, a major part of it, releases CO2 while immobilizing or mineralizing nutrients, so respiration rates track microbial turnover and nitrogen mineralization.
Tillage usually increases soil respiration, depleting soil organic matter.
Between 1989 and 2008 soil respiration increased by about 0.1% per year.
It forms a positive feedback with climate: warming raises respiration and so CO2; a 2 °C rise is estimated to add 10 Pg of carbon a year from soils.

conflicts.text: In 2008 the global total of CO2 released by soil respiration was roughly 98 billion tonnes.
conflicts.note: Carbon cycle gives about 98 billion tonnes for 2008 against 77 Pg of carbon a year on Soil respiration; the Carbon cycle figure may be CO2 rather than carbon.

title: Sources of soil respiration
article: Soil respiration#Sources of carbon dioxide in soil

definition.text: The organisms and pathways that produce the CO2 leaving soil: roots, rhizosphere microbes, decomposers and soil animals.

facts.text: Root respiration accounts for approximately half of all soil respiration, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions.
Up to 20% of photosynthetic carbon enters the soil as root exudates, decomposed mainly by bacteria; mycorrhizal fungi also respire sugars the plant gives them.
The CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration and also from fermentation, which works without oxygen, as in the oxygen-poor rhizosphere.
Soil animals add to it by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, exposing more surface to microbes.

definition.text: The non-living factors, chiefly temperature, soil moisture and nitrogen, that set how fast soil carbon is respired to CO2.

facts.text: Respiration rises exponentially with temperature to a maximum, then falls to zero as enzymes fail; root respiration starts to shut down above 35 °C.
Cryophiles work best below 20 °C, mesophiles between 20 and 40 °C and thermophiles above 40 °C, so mixed communities respire over a broad range.
Respiration is low when dry, peaks at intermediate moisture and falls when water shuts out oxygen.
Nitrogen costs roots energy: taking in nitrate costs 0.4 units of CO2 and reducing it 2 units; nitrogen-rich litter also decomposes faster.

definition.text: Field and laboratory techniques for measuring how fast CO2 leaves the soil and where it comes from.

facts.text: Closed chambers sealed over the soil derive the flux from CO2 build-up over a few minutes (F=bV/A); longer runs underestimate it as CO2 is stored in the soil.
Open systems pump fresh air through the chamber and read the flux at equilibrium; portable survey systems move between soil collars to capture variation from place to place.
Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars.
Stable carbon isotopes separate sources: swapping C3 and C4 crops, or spraying C4 cane sugar, tells old from new carbon and microbial from root respiration.

definition.text: How rising CO2, warming, changing rainfall and nitrogen fertilization are altering soil respiration around the planet.

facts.text: Free air CO2 enrichment (FACE) studies show elevated CO2 raises soil respiration through more roots and microbial activity, by up to 40.6% in sweetgum and poplar forests.
Warming may hit hardest in the Arctic, where thawing permafrost turns aerobic and its large carbon stores are respired much faster.
Dry soils burst into respiration after rain and slow as they dry, so more frequent, intense rain should raise respiration sharply in arid lands.
Nitrogen fertilization since the Green Revolution boosts plant growth, root respiration and root biomass, and with them soil respiration.

title: Birch effect

definition.text: The influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil.

facts.text: Respiration in dry soil usually bursts to a very high level after rainfall, then declines as the soil dries.
Sudden wetting can burst bacterial cells; the released contents feed other bacteria and briefly boost respiration.
Soil microbial communities shift in diversity and composition through drying and rewetting cycles.

notes: No crawled article: Birch effect is listed in the gaps file. Named only on Soil ecology (S:ccbd740605e5); the moisture and rewetting effects on respiration come from Soil respiration and Soil ecology, which do not tie the name to them explicitly.

definition.text: Enzymes in soil, released mainly by microbes, that break down organic matter and free nutrients for plants.

facts.text: Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some; they decompose soil organic matter into humus, releasing nutrients plants need.
They catalyse the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, lignin, starch and urea, making them prominent agents of the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
They may be intracellular, cell-associated or free, and microbes use them to degrade large molecules left by dead plants and animals.
Bound to clay and humic colloids, they are protected from rapid breakdown but less active: a trade-off between protection and activity.
Their distribution is highly patchy, varying at millimetre scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and also from single trees to whole catchments.
Fertilizers may include urease inhibitors to delay the release of nutrients over a longer period.
Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic fertilizers better still.
Their activity both stabilizes and degrades soil structure, and they play a decisive role in maintaining soil health.

title: Earthworm

definition.text: A soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida; the name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta.

facts.text: Found mostly in moist, compost-rich soil, earthworms eat detritus along with protozoa, nematodes, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important detritivores.
Adults range from 10 mm long to 3 m, but the typical Lumbricus terrestris grows to about 360 mm.
They move by waves of muscle contraction anchored by bristles called setae, and breathe through their moist skin, having no special respiratory organs.
Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture; most favour neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them.
Their activity aerates and mixes soil, favours nutrient mineralization and uptake by plants, and links organic matter to soil minerals.
They are indicators of soil health: healthy soil holds more earthworms, and their gut microbes reveal the condition of the soil.
Nitrogen fertilizers create acidity fatal to worms and pesticides kill them; at least three species are listed as extinct and many more endangered.
In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world.

definition.text: The grouping of earthworms by where they live and feed: epigeic, endogeic and anecic.

facts.text: Epigeic worms live in leaf litter or compost at the soil-litter interface, do not burrow and eat decomposing organic matter; Eisenia fetida is one.
Endogeic worms live in topsoil or subsoil, eat soil and make horizontal burrows in the upper 10–30 cm.
Anecic worms ('reaching up'), such as Lumbricus terrestris, build permanent deep vertical burrows and come up to gather leaves, mixing surface organic matter into mineral soil.
Epigeic Eisenia species suit vermicomposting because they eat fresh organic matter without burrowing and tolerate the heat of compost heaps.
Healthy soil holds a larger number and biomass of earthworms, especially endogeic and anecic species.

title: Earthworms and soil fertility

definition.text: The biological, chemical and physical ways earthworm activity improves soil for plants, by fragmenting, mixing, grinding and digesting plant debris.

facts.text: Anecic worms pull leaf fall and manure into their burrows, shred it and mix it with soil, turning it into humus; casts can hold 40 percent more humus than the top 230 mm of soil.
Grit in the gizzard grinds swallowed particles, sand grains up to 1.3 mm included, into a paste whose large surface favours microbes and enzymes.
Casts are richer in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus than the bulk soil, with nutrients in plant-available form; where humus is plentiful, one worm may produce over 4.5 kilograms of casts a year.
Burrows keep soil structured, aerated and drained, and earthworms speed the formation of water-stable macroaggregates.
Darwin estimated up to 53,000 worms per acre of arable land; newer figures run from 250,000 per acre on poor soil to 1,750,000 per acre on rich farmland.
Richly organic topsoil averages 500 earthworms per square metre, weighing up to 400 g/m2.
Whether worms hasten the loss of organic matter as CO2 or preserve it as humus was long debated; a consensus now credits them with carbon sequestration, as most is stabilized deep with clay.
Their greenhouse gas emissions, direct or through soil microbes, are not fully quantified but likely add to global warming.

title: Earthworm invasions

definition.text: The spread of a few earthworm species, carried by people, into regions where they are not native.

facts.text: Of around 7,000 earthworm species, only about 150 are widely distributed: the peregrine or cosmopolitan earthworms.
Of the 308 earthworm taxa in the United States and Canada, 70 (23%) are introduced species.
In podzols, invading earthworms can erase the banded profile, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.
Surface-dwelling earthworms speed up carbon cycling and have been spread by humans into many new regions.
Peregrine earthworms spread through intentional and accidental transport of plants and soil, helped by growing trade, and can carry viruses and spores of plant pathogens.
Jumping worms, pheretimoid earthworms of Amynthas, Metaphire and Pheretima native to Australia and East Asia, commonly harm the places they invade.
In the UK the invasive New Zealand flatworm feeds on earthworms, and other earthworm populations declined after it appeared.
No known method removes earthworms from soil; buying heat-treated compost and removing shrubs such as buckthorn, whose litter worms favour, slow or reduce them.

definition.text: Feeding organic waste to earthworms to turn it into vermicompost.

facts.text: It usually uses the brandling worm Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil; in the tropics the African nightcrawler and Indian blue are used.
Vermicompost, also called worm castings or worm humus, is the end product of earthworms breaking down organic matter.
Earthworms fed partly composted material excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available to plants.
Added to soil, ideally as a surface mulch, the humified material improves moisture and nutrient availability and benefits soil microbes.

definition.text: A small pile, coil or pellet of soil or sand that burrowing worms expel at the surface.

facts.text: Worms swallow soil with its organic matter and microbes; digestion breaks up mineral particles and partly decomposes organic matter, and the rest is pushed out through the burrow.
On lawns and grasslands, earthworm casts are taken as a sign of biologically active, healthy soil.
Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the surrounding soil and build stable soil aggregates.
On beaches and tidal flats, burrowing polychaete worms leave coiled, spaghetti-like casts.

definition.text: The part of the soil shaped by earthworm secretions, burrowing and casts: soil that has passed through their gut or lines their burrows.

facts.text: The burrow lining averages 2 mm thick but can reach about 8 mm around the burrows of litter-feeding earthworms.
It is generally richer in nitrogen, phosphorus and humified organic matter than the surrounding soil, probably because earthworms prefer to eat leaf and root litter.
In one soil it held 40 per cent of the aerobic and 13 per cent of the anaerobic nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and 16 per cent of the denitrifiers.
Through it earthworms steer soil microbial communities and with them organic matter and nutrient dynamics.

definition.text: The reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains.

facts.text: Bioturbation profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity.
Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaetes, shrimps and midge larvae dominate.
It differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and solutes in sediments, which is one of its effects.
Burrowers carry oxygen into reduced layers, changing microbial metabolism and speeding organic matter decomposition, and their burrows shelter other species.
Darwin began its formal study in the 1800s: chalk spread on a field lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year he credited to earthworms.
Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees in 1891, Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil and geomorphology literature since the 1980s.
Since its onset around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion.
When pollution harms soil engineers such as earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the humus form shifts toward mor.

definition.text: The mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and by plant roots, which matters for soil production, burial, organic matter content and downslope transport.

facts.text: Plants and animals disturb the upper soil and bring weathered rock, saprolite, up from depth to the surface.
Tree roots add organic matter and leave voids when they rot, and uprooted trees throw up mounds and can invert sections of soil.
Burrows of earthworms and small mammals carry air and water and change particle-size distribution with depth, porosity and nutrient content.
Detritus-eating burrowers build the organic-rich topsoil called the soil biomantle and so help form soil horizons.
Pocket gophers may produce soil on a scale equal to abiotic processes; their mounds bring little-weathered rock to the surface, speeding soil formation, and are easily eroded downslope.
Mounds bury vegetation that decays into nutrient hotspots, and burrows, even backfilled, lower soil density.

definition.text: The disturbance of archaeological layers by burrowing organisms, which blurs the order in which deposits were laid down.

facts.text: Archaeologists date finds relatively by stratigraphy, in which the topmost layer is the youngest.
By moving material up, down and sideways, bioturbation confuses the archaeological record and makes relative dating harder.
It is studied by archaeologists alongside geologists and biologists.

title: Biofilm

definition.text: A community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS).

facts.text: The EPS matrix combines polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water.
Called 'cities for microbes', biofilms let residents share nutrients and shelter them; cells inside differ physiologically from free-floating (planktonic) cells of the same organism.
The matrix keeps extracellular enzymes close to the cells, working as an external digestion system, and carries chemical signals and gene exchange.
In soil and on plant surfaces most bacteria live bound in biofilms; soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces.
Root biofilms of plant growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and Azospirillum can prime plants' systemic resistance to pathogens.
Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen; their internal gradients let nitrifiers work near the surface while anoxic microbes deeper inside denitrify.
Microbial activity in the matrix can precipitate calcium carbonate, a form of biomineralization.
In soil, biofilms can cause bioclogging; in sewage works and slow sand filters they are used to strip pollutants from water.

notes: Medical, dental, food-industry, shipping and gut sections skipped as out of scope.

definition.text: The microbial developmental process by which a biofilm forms, summarized in five major stages.

facts.text: It starts with reversible attachment of free-floating cells to a surface, held first by weak van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects.
Attachment becomes irreversible as cells anchor with structures such as pili and further cells aggregate.
Stages three and four are maturation, with cell clusters embedded in matrix growing into micro-colonies.
The fifth stage, dispersal, releases cells that colonize new surfaces.

definition.text: A heterotroph that gets its nutrients by eating detritus: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces.

facts.text: Detritivores swallow discrete lumps of matter, unlike decomposers such as bacteria and fungi, which absorb food at a molecular scale; the two terms are often confused.
Typical soil detritivores include millipedes, springtails, woodlice, slugs and many worms.
They carry out the first stage of remineralization by fragmenting dead plant matter, letting decomposers complete the second.
Plant litter does not pile up in nature because of them, even though cellulose, lignin and xylan decay much more slowly than other organic molecules.
Together with decomposers they return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil for plants to use.
Detritus feeders mainly digest the protein-rich microbes growing on detritus and excrete the detritus itself little changed.
Moist soil increases their feeding and excretion; in deserts they shelter in burrows and are the main clearers of plant litter.
In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria could not yet digest lignin, so dead plant tissue piled up and later became fossil fuels.

definition.text: Mostly soil-dwelling bacteria that feed on dead organic matter, digesting it outside the cell with enzymes and absorbing the products.

facts.text: Alongside saprotrophic fungi and water molds they drive decomposition and nutrient cycling, feeding higher trophic levels.
Bacteria outcompete fungi for easily available substrates, but their higher nitrogen demand and inability to move nutrients make them less efficient decomposers in forest soils.
Their community make-up and growth rates are used as signals of soil health, since growth responds quickly to environmental change.
Some are pathogens spread through contact with excrement, such as Escherichia coli; others ferment cellulose in the rumen of cows.

title: Soil bacterial growth rates

definition.text: How fast soil bacteria produce new biomass and replace their populations, a measure that responds quickly to changing conditions.

facts.text: Under normal conditions bacterial biomass production stays fairly steady, growth being balanced by predation and other deaths.
Leucine or thymidine incorporation suggests turnover in days to weeks at around 20 °C, while other studies estimate 107–160 days at 25 °C, a gap put down to methods and temperature.
Root exudates make the rhizosphere a special case, with turnover estimated at just 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots.
Growth rises with soil moisture, and added glucose boosts it at low concentrations but inhibits it at very high ones.

notes: S:c4d9a890c387 and S:4185bc921685 carry CITATION NEEDED. S:8c4446514244 itself reports the two turnover estimates and calls the gap a large discrepancy due to method and temperature.

title: Enzymatic latch

definition.text: The control of decomposition in peat by phenol oxidases: by breaking down phenolics that inhibit hydrolase enzymes, they release decay, so limits on the microbes limit decomposition.

facts.text: Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) to break down soil organic matter when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs indicate nutrient availability.
Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.
β-glucosidase releases sugars that give microbes energy and labile carbon.
Acid and alkaline phosphatases indicate the potential for phosphorus mineralization in soil.

notes: Anchored on the section about microbial extracellular enzymes; general soil enzyme facts are on the Soil enzyme entry.

title: Lithotroph

definition.text: An organism that takes the electrons it needs for building its cells or making energy from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic matter.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek lithos (rock) and troph (consumer), so lithotrophs are 'eaters of rock'; Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946.
In the broad sense lithotrophs include light-using photolithotrophs such as plants, but chemolithotrophs are exclusively microorganisms, all in the domains Bacteria and Archaea.
The opposite strategy is the organotroph, which gets its reducing agents by breaking down organic compounds.

Lithoautotrophs take their carbon from carbon dioxide in the air as plants do; lithoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon dioxide and must consume organic compounds, and only a few bacteria are fully lithoheterotrophic.
Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, taking up organic material to supplement the carbon they fix from carbon dioxide.
They live in deep terrestrial subsurfaces, soils, mines and rock-dwelling endolith communities, and take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements.
In the iron cycle they can use iron either as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).
The last universal common ancestor of life is thought to have been a chemolithotroph.

notes: Two Biogeochemical cycling sentences look wrong in the source: S:383b32fbfb13 calls ammonium 'organic nitrogen', and S:1d66ed5fdf7f says denitrification turns ammonium into nitrogen gas (the table row S:d4a1cc8a85a5 gives that reaction to anammox bacteria). Neither is used here.

title: Chemolithotrophy

definition.text: A way of living in which a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds, such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen.

facts.text: The oxidation is coupled to ATP synthesis: electrons taken from the inorganic donor are passed into respiratory chains that make ATP.
Most chemolithotrophs are chemolithoautotrophs that fix carbon dioxide, usually through the Calvin cycle, an energetically expensive pathway.
The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and nitrifying bacteria: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate.
Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor of the best-documented forms, but nitrate and other organic and inorganic acceptors are also used, and the list of anaerobic chemolithotrophs is growing.
Energy yields differ by substrate: oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol).
On low-energy substrates such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places.
Because chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build organic matter in the dark, and some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.
Sergei Winogradsky first characterized this metabolism, discovering the first known form of lithotrophy while working with Beggiatoa in 1887.

notes: Also on Soil biology (S:01d22d9d05de, nitrification), Microorganism (S:3516dd721bcd) and Nitrifying bacteria (S:823efc0790f9).

definition.text: The part that rock-colonizing lithotrophs, cyanobacteria above all, play in starting soil formation on bare rock.

facts.text: Cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixing photolithotrophs: they use energy from sunlight and inorganic nutrients from rock as reductants.
This lets them grow on native, nutrient-poor rock and leave behind organic matter that other organisms can then colonize.
Colonization can start the decomposition of organic compounds, a primary factor in soil genesis, and the mechanism is thought to have helped shape the early biological Earth.
Lithoautotrophs take part in weathering bedrock into soil and in cycling sulfur, potassium and other elements, freeing nutrients that sustain life.

title: Acid mine drainage

definition.text: The acid runoff made when lithotrophic microbes in mining areas oxidize pyrite and other reduced sulfur minerals to sulfate.

facts.text: The acidophilic bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, for example, uses iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which can drain from the mine with runoff.
It drives the pH of groundwater and streams down to 2–3, changes their chemistry and may endanger plant and animal populations downstream.
The same kind of activity runs on a much smaller scale in nature: in soil and talus, on glacier beds, on stone buildings and monuments, and in the deep subsurface.

notes: No Acid mine drainage article was crawled; the section anchor is the only source. Also mentioned on Rhizofiltration (S:c5bc4efcb57f).

title: Oligotroph

definition.text: An organism able to live where nutrients are available only at very low levels.

facts.text: The word joins the Greek oligos ('few') and trophikos ('feeding'); oligotrophs are contrasted with copiotrophs, which prefer nutrient-rich environments.
They grow slowly, have low metabolic rates and generally live at low population densities.

'Oligotrophic' describes land and water with very low concentrations of nitrates, iron, phosphates and carbon sources, such as deep ocean sediments, caves, polar ice, aquifers, deep subsurface soil and leached soils.
They survive scarcity by switching on genes during low-nutrient periods, but excess nutrients overwhelm their metabolism, and their enzymes struggle in rich conditions.
Lichens, with their extremely low metabolic rate, and the cave-dwelling olm are examples of oligotrophic organisms.
Elevated carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth, slow the soil carbon cycle and favour oligotrophs, which are slower-growing and more resource-efficient than copiotrophs.

notes: Copiotroph now has its own entry. Mycorrhiza (S:df1eec50901a) and Bog (S:cec3bebe246f) also use the term.

definition.text: Soils, such as farmed and frozen soils, in which microbes have very few nutrients to live on.

facts.text: Nutrients thin out with depth because surface microbes quickly consume what decomposes from plant and animal debris, and their metabolic wastes build up toxic chemicals lower down.
Water and oxygen diffuse less easily as depth increases; aggregates, pores and extracellular enzymes help water, oxygen and nutrients move into the soil.
Frozen polar soils are dominated by Actinomycetota, Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Cyanobacteria; Actinomycetota keep their enzymes working across a wide range of low temperatures.
The bacterium Collimonas lives in such soils by digesting chitin from fungi and by weathering rocks and minerals for electron sources.

definition.text: The ways plants of oligotrophic soils take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them.

facts.text: Uptake improves through root adaptations such as nitrogen-fixing root nodules, mycorrhizae and cluster roots.
Plants grow very slowly and use abundant ions for turgor while saving scarce nutrients for building tissue; many store nutrients, in trunk tissue for example, and remobilize them when demand rises.
On the ancient sandplains and lateritic soils of southern Western Australia, most plants rely on cluster roots for phosphorus and sulfur, yet the vegetation is highly diverse.
White-sand soils of the Rio Negro basin in northern Amazonia, with pH below 5.0, carry low-diversity, extremely fragile forests and savannahs.

title: Biomineralization

definition.text: The process by which living organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often hardening or stiffening their tissues.

facts.text: It is extremely widespread: every major lineage of the biosphere has mineral-forming members, and over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms.
Most biominerals are silicates, carbonates or phosphates: silica in algae, diatoms and sponges, carbonates in invertebrates, and calcium phosphates and carbonates in vertebrates.
The most common are calcium phosphate and carbonate salts, used with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin to give bones and shells their structural support.
Bacteria take part in copper, iron and gold deposits; microorganisms can precipitate metals from solution and can also catalyse the dissolution of minerals.
It plays global roles in shaping the planet, in biogeochemical cycles and as a carbon sink.
Bicarbonate released by weathering and carried through soil to the sea is biomineralized there into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons.
Microbes can clean uranium-contaminated groundwater by releasing phosphate, which precipitates uranium phosphate minerals and so reduces the uranium's mobility.
The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

notes: The dossier definition line S:ca9e5e5b41a9 quotes a different sense (complete conversion of organic substances to inorganic derivatives by organisms), which is mineralization in the soil-science sense and belongs to Mineralization (soil science); the lead sentence S:6c45587ae9f5 is used instead.

definition.text: A scheme that sorts mineral formation by living things according to how much the organism controls it: biomineralization proper, organomineralization and inorganic mineralization.

facts.text: In biologically controlled mineralization the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location, as in mollusc and brachiopod shells.

In biologically induced mineralization microbial metabolism creates chemical conditions that favour mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete, as in stromatolites and other microbial mats.
In biologically influenced mineralization abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals.
The terms have no standardized definitions and their use varies widely; this scheme follows a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues.

title: Geomycology

definition.text: The study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals.

facts.text: Fungi deposit minerals on an organic matrix, such as a protein, that offers a nucleation site; proteins they secrete control the size and shape of the carbonate minerals they precipitate.
Using organic phosphorus, fungi can precipitate uranium-bearing phosphate minerals and gather them in their mycelium; species such as Aspergillus niger and Paecilomyces javanicus tolerate uranium.
Fungi also break minerals down, mainly strains that produce oxalic acid: Aspergillus niger, Serpula himantioides and Trametes versicolor corrode apatite and galena.

title: Biogenic mineral controversy

definition.text: The dispute over whether crystalline substances made by living things should count as minerals.

facts.text: The geological definition of a mineral normally excludes compounds found only in living beings, yet calcite is often biogenic and organisms make hydroxylapatite, which also occurs in rocks.
The International Mineralogical Association, the recognized standard body, accepted 5,650 official mineral species out of 5,862 proposed or traditional ones as of December 2020.

Lowenstam (1981) noted that organisms form some minerals that cannot form inorganically; Skinner (2005) counts any element or compound, amorphous or crystalline, formed through biogeochemical processes as a mineral.
Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, down to at least 1,600 metres below the sea floor.

contested_note: Geologists and mineralogists disagree over the International Mineralogical Association's decision to exclude biogenic crystalline substances from the list of minerals.
notes: S:20d4427847db carries CITATION NEEDED. Mineral#Definitions > Biogenic minerals (what-soil-is-made-of) repeats much of this section (S:b2ec668cfc81, S:9a42eb080c98, S:58309c1b523c); merge if that chapter drafts it.

definition.text: A biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil matrix.

facts.text: The main microbes that can induce it are photosynthetic cyanobacteria and microalgae, sulfate-reducing bacteria and some species involved in the nitrogen cycle.

Bacteria can trigger it by urea hydrolysis, denitrification, sulfate production or iron reduction; autotrophic pathways deplete carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the nitrogen and sulfur cycles.

In ureolysis, microbial urease splits urea into ammonium and carbonate; the hydroxide ions formed raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate, which precipitates with calcium as calcium carbonate crystals.
A first layer of calcite makes bacteria cling more strongly to the soil surface, so further calcite layers build up.
Calcium carbonate can precipitate as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability; such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian.
Proposed uses include repairing cracks in concrete and preventing its corrosion, biogrout, and sequestering radionuclides and heavy metals.
Contaminant metals and radionuclides are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and chelation with the precipitate reduces the availability of lead in soil.

title: Biocementation of soil

definition.text: The use of microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation as a cementing technique to strengthen sand that might otherwise liquefy.

facts.text: Treated sand gains shear strength, compressive strength, stiffness and liquefaction resistance because grains are bonded and the soil becomes denser; triaxial tests on bio-cemented Ottawa sand showed shear strength rising by a factor of 1.8.

Strength comes mostly from point-to-point contacts between carbonate crystals and sand grains, so trickling solution from the surface, which forms crystals at grain bridges, gives more strength per amount of calcite.
It could be a cheap, green alternative to chemical grouting, whose synthetic additives are costly and, except for sodium silicate, toxic.

Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm, so the method suits soils with few fines (USCS GW, GP, SW, SP, ML and organic soils); enriching native ureolytic bacteria in place can help.

notes: S:44a71a7cb760 says treatment 'may be limited to deep soil', which seems to contradict the following sentences about shallow depths; not used.

title: Soil-borne pathogen

definition.text: A disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host and tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil.

facts.text: Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and nematodes such as Meloidogyne.
Fungi are among them, although other soil fungi are beneficial plant partners such as mycorrhizae.
Their propagules can be stirred to germinate by plant exudates in the laimosphere and start the hypocotyl and stem rots that cause damping-off.
Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring soil-borne diseases along with acidification and degradation, lowering productivity.
Fallowing disrupts them by temporarily removing their hosts, and soil solarization heats the soil until many are killed or greatly weakened.
Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, mycorrhizal plants often resist them, and compost teas have a suppressive effect on soil-borne diseases.
Hydroponics, which grows roots in substrates instead of soil, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests.

notes: The page itself is two sentences; the other facts come from Laimosphere, Soil microbiology, Soil acidification, Fallow, Soil solarization, Disease suppressive soils, Mycorrhiza, Compost and Hydroponics.

title: Microbial inoculant

definition.text: An agricultural amendment, also called a soil inoculant or bioinoculant, that uses beneficial rhizosphere or endophytic microbes to promote plant health.

facts.text: Many of the microbes form mutualistic partnerships with the crop; besides improving nutrition they can promote growth by stimulating plant hormone production.

Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting rhizobacteria, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers; Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules, is the most commonly applied.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus: in one reduced-fertilization greenhouse, AM fungi with rhizobacteria gave the tomato yields of 100% fertility at 70% fertility.
Inoculants can induce systemic acquired resistance in crops, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot.
Mixing strains raises plant nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer, and several strains together raise nitrogenase activity even when only one fixes nitrogen.
Inoculants often change the existing soil microbial community.

Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial; with commercial products mycorrhizal colonization was under 10%, though an estimated 836 million USD is spent on inoculants each year.
They are not widely used in industrial agriculture because large-scale application is not yet economically viable.

notes: Overlaps Biofertilizer (fertilizers-manures-and-amendments); the 2024 and global-study sentences (S:48063d0d0843, S:8c4e630b5fde) question commercial products but the source does not call the matter disputed.

title: Ammonia fungi

definition.text: Fungi whose fruiting bodies develop quickly and germinate readily when ammonia or other nitrogen-rich material makes the soil alkaline.

facts.text: They appear naturally after decomposition events such as animal excretion or death, and heavy additions of ammonia or urea create the conditions they thrive in until the soil reverts.
Most live in temperate forests on well-rotted wood, plant debris or dung, and they are most active in the O horizon, then the A and B horizons.
Adding ammonia or urea raises the pH of soil litter to 8–10, which interrupts nutrient recycling; soil ammonia takes up to 2 years to return to its earlier level, helped by late-phase fungi.
They help maintain the nitrogen cycle, and some are predators: Laccaria bicolor catches and kills springtails.

notes: S:f83e842d4b5d (ammonia fungi reduce greenhouse gas through denitrification) and S:9d6f57926bfa (mycorrhizal networks fix nitrogen) look doubtful and are not used.

definition.text: The order in which ammonia fungi fruit after ammonia or urea reaches forest soil, divided into early-phase and late-phase groups.

facts.text: Anamorphic fungi come first, tolerating pH above 8; once they bring the pH to 7, cup fungi (Ascomycota) develop, and at pH 6 small basidiomycetes follow.
Early-phase fungi fruit 20 to 200 days after urea is applied, in alkaline to neutral soils rich in ammonium-nitrogen, and usually run only one cycle.
Late-phase agarics with larger fruiting bodies develop once the pH is 3.5–6.0, typically 2–3 years after application, and gradually turn soil ammonium into nitrate-nitrogen.
Late-phase fungi are larger and more numerous, can recur over several cycles, and are mostly biotrophic, with few saprobic species.

title: Petrichor

definition.text: The earthy scent often noticed when rain falls on dry soil or rock.

facts.text: Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Grenfell Thomas introduced the term in a 1964 Nature paper for what had been called 'argillaceous odour', from the Greek petra (rock) and ichor, the fluid in the gods' veins.

It is a mixture of volatiles: oils from plant matter build up on mineral surfaces in dry spells and are pushed out of rock and soil pores by moisture, joined by microbial geosmin and 2-methylisoborneol.
The scent offers a glimpse of the soil atmosphere: after a drought, infiltrating rainwater flushes the soil air out.
Pliny the Elder noted the pleasant smell of earth when rain follows drought and took it as a sign of fertile soil.
In 1891 Marcellin Berthelot and G. André steam-distilled an odorous substance from soil but could not identify it.
In 1965 Bear and Thomas reported that small amounts of the oily extracts delay seed germination and early plant growth.
High-speed filming at MIT in 2015 showed raindrops on porous surfaces trap air bubbles that burst as aerosols, and light or moderate rain made more aerosols than heavy rain.
A 2026 study in dryland soils reaching into the Negev Desert found 58 volatile organic compounds released on rewetting, which may feed atmospheric ozone and secondary aerosol formation.

notes: The CONTESTED flag on S:75b29a058141 is Phipson's own uncertainty about whether his 1865 notes were published, not a debate.

title: Geosmin

definition.text: A chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek geō- ('earth') and osmē ('smell'); Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968.
It is a secondary metabolite of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces.
It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor, the smell of rain after dry weather or of disturbed soil.
People smell it at very low levels, from 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per litre of water; the natural (−) form, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L, is about eight times more potent.
With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide; it is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid.
It attracts springtails, which feed on Streptomyces and spread its spores, and repels the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
Standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation.

conflicts.text: Humans detect geosmin at concentrations as low as anywhere from 400 parts per trillion to 5 parts per trillion.
conflicts.note: A wider and partly higher range than the lead's 0.006–0.01 micrograms per litre; Petrichor (S:9e9ddb7c941c) notes measured thresholds vary with experimental conditions.

notes: The dossier definition line S:489af83b4458 is chembox boilerplate; the lead sentences S:7db4bfb05785 and S:4065f98694a4 define the compound.

title: Bacterial metabolic types

definition.text: The grouping of bacteria by their source of energy, the electron donors they use and their source of carbon.

facts.text: Phototrophs get their energy from light by photosynthesis, while chemotrophs get it by oxidizing chemical compounds.
Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are lithotrophs; those that use organic compounds are organotrophs.
Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide.
Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide; facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

notes: No Primary nutritional groups page was crawled; this section is the only general source for the scheme.

title: Total organic carbon

definition.text: An analytical measure of the concentration of organic carbon in a sample.

facts.text: Total carbon is the organic carbon plus the inorganic carbon, such as that in carbonate minerals; analysers measure only total carbon, so the inorganic part is subtracted or first driven off with acid.

The sample's carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, for example by combustion at 1000 up to 1200 °C or on a catalyst at 680 up to 950 °C, and most modern analysers read the gas by non-dispersive infrared.
Soil organic matter content can be calculated from it; in the UK, guideline values for pollutants such as phenol and toluene depend on that content.
It also serves as a non-specific indicator of water quality and is the first chemical analysis made on potential petroleum source rock.

notes: Assigned to this chapter by the graph, but it fits soil-carbon-and-climate or soil-survey better; the page is mostly about water and petroleum analysis.

title: Lumbricus terrestris

definition.text: A large, reddish earthworm, known as the common earthworm, lob worm or nightcrawler, thought to be native to Western Europe and now spread around the world.

facts.text: Generally 110–200 millimetres long and 7–10 millimetres across, with around 120–170 segments, it is the largest naturally occurring earthworm through much of Europe.
A deep-burrowing anecic worm, it builds vertical burrows, pulls surface litter down into the mineral soil and leaves casts of mixed organic and mineral material on the surface.
Where it has invaded podzols it has erased their banded profile of litter, pale E and coloured B horizons, leaving thin litter and a dark, worm-mixed Ap horizon over the B.
It is invasive in the north central United States, thriving in fence rows and woodlots and reducing native plant and tree regrowth, though it fares poorly in tilled fields.

notes: A single species assigned by the graph; it passes only the own-article test. Its 20–25 cm extended length (S:4b2608308a88) and 110–200 mm general length (S:0f87769efa9d) measure different states, so they are not treated as a conflict.
