title: Extracellular polymeric substance

definition.text: High-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms secrete into their surroundings.

facts.text: They are mostly polysaccharides and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic substances, and make up 50% to 90% of a biofilm's total organic matter.
They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials.
Exopolysaccharides help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, which matters for colonizing roots and the rhizosphere.
Together with microbial cells, EPS can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity.
EPS make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates.
They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps in bioremediation of heavy metals.
EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger remove polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

notes: Much of the page is about microalgal EPS in industry and medicine; only the soil-relevant parts are used.

title: Dwarf forest

definition.text: An uncommon ecosystem of miniature trees, also called elfin or pygmy forest, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards.

facts.text: Dwarf forests usually grow at high elevations where the air is humid but the soil is poor; the two main types are coastal temperate and montane tropical.
Tropical montane elfin forests have small trees, 5–8 m tall, with shallow roots and abundant epiphytes; high winds largely set their stature.
At 6,834 hectares, the pygmy forest of Mount Hamiguitan in the Philippines is the largest known dwarf forest in the country and possibly the world.

notes: Assigned by the graph; its soil interest lies in the coastal pygmy forests, drafted separately as Mendocino ecological staircase.

title: Mendocino ecological staircase

definition.text: A flight of uplifted marine terraces on the northern California coast, each about 100,000 years older than the one below and carrying its own soils, microbes, plants and animals.

facts.text: Plant succession repeated on each terrace eventually forms a very acid, nutrient-poor podzol, the Blacklock series, with a clay or iron hardpan beneath.
Pygmy forest soils are low in macro- and micronutrients and high in exchangeable aluminium, and the iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage.
Pines there are rarely more than three or four feet high, with inch-thick trunks holding 80 or more growth rings, while the same species grows many dozens of feet high on younger soils nearby.

Hans Jenny studied the pygmy forest on a 500,000-year-old terrace, and the sequence shows one soil passing through several successive steady states; the site became the Pygmy Forest National Natural Landmark in 1974.

notes: A soil chronosequence example; how-soils-form (Chronosequence) may want to cite it.

definition.text: Nematodes (thread worms) that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside their hosts.

facts.text: They attack insects living in the soil, such as the larvae of moths, butterflies, flies and beetles, and adult beetles, grasshoppers and crickets.

An infective juvenile enters an insect and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it within 24–48 hours; after about a week hundreds of thousands of new juveniles leave the cadaver.

Ambushers such as Steinernema carpocapsae wait at the surface and infect surface insects, while cruisers such as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora hunt deeper, so tillage cut the first's numbers but left the second's unchanged.

Steinernematids and heterorhabditids are used in biological pest control: together they cut plum curculio populations by as much as 70–90% in northeastern American orchards, though they fail against foliage pests because UV light and drying harm them.

definition.text: In lawn care, a layer of organic matter that builds up around the base of the grass plants.

facts.text: It is a mix of living and dead crowns, stolons, rhizomes and roots, about 25% of it lignin, which resists decay; grass clippings add little because soil microbes break them down easily.
It builds up when acid soils cannot support enough decomposers, when insecticides cut earthworm activity and so bioturbation, or when excess nitrogen fertilizer spurs growth and acidifies the soil.
A thin layer insulates against swings in temperature and moisture, but too much causes root problems and mowing difficulties and is removed with a dethatcher.

definition.text: Springtails (class Collembola) are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth.

facts.text: More than 9,000 species are known; they are omnivorous, free-living and prefer moist conditions.
They do not decompose organic matter directly but speed decomposition by fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbial communities.
They mostly eat fungal hyphae and spores, but also plant material, pollen, animal remains and bacteria; geosmin from Streptomyces attracts some species, which eat and spread its spores.
Estimates reach 100,000 individuals per square metre; temperate deciduous woodland litter typically holds 30 to 40 species, and the tropics may exceed 100.
Species assemblages change with depth from canopy to litter to deeper soil horizons, and across landscapes with soil acidity, moisture and light; as a group they are highly sensitive to drying out.
They are prey for mesostigmatan mites and soil centipedes, and escape by jumping with a spring-like furcula, which is hard to do inside soil.

Folsomia candida is used in standardized toxicity and avoidance tests for soil pollution; unlike earthworms, springtails are very sensitive to herbicides, and they serve as bioindicators of soil quality.
In lawns and turfgrass they act as 'thatch busters', helping decompose the thatch layer between the green vegetation and the soil surface.

image.caption: Mvuijlst, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: Oribatid mites, also called moss or beetle mites, are a group of slow-living mites that are the most prevalent arthropods in forest soils.

facts.text: They measure 0.2 to 1.4 millimetres; about 12,000 species are described, and estimates of the total run from 60,000 to 120,000.
They are essential for breaking down organic detritus and distributing fungi, feeding on living and dead plant and fungal material, lichens and carrion; none is parasitic.
Like earthworms they speed the breakdown of organic material, but unlike many earthworms they do not mix it with mineral matter; some mine conifer needles from inside.
They have low metabolic rates, slow development and low fecundity, taking months to two years to mature in temperate forest soils, and are densest in forests with thick organic layers.

definition.text: Enchytraeids are a family of small, earthworm-like oligochaete worms; the terrestrial species, called potworms, live in highly organic soils.

facts.text: Over 700 species are described; most are whitish or transparent worms a few millimetres long that eat decaying organic matter and its microbes, aiding decomposition and nutrient cycling.
Like earthworms they are ecosystem engineers, shaping soil structure by creating aggregates of various sizes.
They feed on earthworm casts and turn them into fluffy masses of their own faeces, which make up the bulk of the OH horizon of moder humus.
Less sensitive than earthworms to farming intensification, they replace them in soils with heavy pesticide use and serve in standard ecotoxicity tests (ISO 16387).

definition.text: An organism found in environments rich in nutrients, especially carbon.

facts.text: Copiotrophs are the opposite of oligotrophs and grow at organic substrate levels up to 100 times higher.

Soil bacterial phyla can be sorted into copiotrophic and oligotrophic groups; soils rich in organic carbon favour copiotrophs, key players in the soil carbon cycle when plants exude simple compounds such as sugars.
They live a 'feast-and-famine' life: motile and chemotactic, they rush to nutrients and use them fast, but survive poorly once supplies run out, when oligotrophs outcompete them.
They grow fast, carrying up to fifteen ribosomal RNA operons against one in oligotrophs, but use carbon less efficiently.

definition.text: The idea that, in arid ecosystems, soil fungi link the activity of plants and biological soil crusts, which respond to different amounts of soil moisture.

facts.text: It proposes that carbon and nutrients stay cycling in living pools rather than being leached or lost to the air between rain pulses.
Fungi can work at higher temperatures and lower water potentials than bacteria, so they likely drive nutrient cycling in hot, dry ecosystems.
Crusts wake after small rains; fungi hold their nutrients until larger rains activate plants, which then pass carbon back to their fungal partners.
Direct tests remain rare, but one isotope study found nitrogen moving up to 100 cm per day in both directions between plants and crust.

definition.text: Roundworms or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda, most of them free-living microbe feeders but many parasitic.

facts.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion per person, with the highest densities in tundra and boreal forests.
Often exceeding a million individuals per square metre, they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth.
About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm of soil.
They do not decompose organic matter but feed on living material; eating up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, they regulate bacterial numbers and community composition.
Through nitrogen mineralization they can play an important role in the nitrogen cycle.
Nematophagous fungi prey on them, trapping them with lassos or adhesive structures or releasing toxins on contact.
Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million.
The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism, and a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

definition.text: Pest nematodes that attack crop plants, chiefly their roots, or spread plant viruses between them.

facts.text: They take about 10% of crops worldwide each year; major genera include Meloidogyne (root-knot), Globodera and Heterodera (cyst) and Pratylenchus (lesion) nematodes.
Root-knot nematodes leave visible galls on roots that help diagnose them in the field, and species such as Xiphinema index carry plant viruses.
Controls include rotation with resistant crops, marigold cover crops and antagonistic fungi and bacteria; Brassica juncea green manure cut densities 13- to 14-fold in CSIRO plots.
Soil steaming kills nematodes before planting but removes harmful and beneficial soil fauna alike.

definition.text: Single-celled amoeboid protists partly enclosed in a shell, or test, with an opening through which their pseudopodia emerge.

facts.text: The test is either made by the cell itself, organic, siliceous or calcareous, or glued together from sediment particles it collects.
They live in most fresh waters, mires and soils; in soil the shell protects them from drying, and they may stay encysted until conditions improve.
Their tough tests survive after death, and some species respond to temperature, pH and conductivity, so they serve as bioindicators and paleoclimate proxies.
Sampled with pollen and plant remains in soil horizons, they can reveal climate or land-use changes during soil formation.

definition.text: An organism that gets its energy and nutrients mainly or entirely by eating bacteria.

facts.text: The term is used mostly for free-living microscopic heterotrophs such as nematodes, amoebae and other protozoa, though some larger invertebrates, certain arthropods among them, also eat bacteria.
Many are generalist predators of any bacteria, but not all bacteria are easily digested; spores of some species, such as Clostridium perfringens, are never eaten.
Springtails and many protozoa are listed among bacterivores.
Bacterivores contaminating environmental samples hinder the growing of bacteria for study; cycloheximide can suppress them but also inhibits some anaerobic prokaryotes.

title: Fungivory

definition.text: Fungivory or mycophagy is the eating of fungi; organisms that eat nothing else are called fungivores.

facts.text: Fungus eaters include birds, mammals, insects, plants, amoebae, snails and slugs, nematodes, bacteria and other fungi.

Mycoparasitic Trichoderma fungi detect other fungi, bind to their hyphae and digest their cell walls with enzymes such as chitinases; they have protected crops from pathogens such as Rhizoctonia solani.
Bacterial mycophagy, a term coined in 2005, is bacteria growing at the expense of living fungal hyphae; most of what is known concerns bacteria and fungi in soil and around plants.
Beetles, ants and termites each evolved fungus farming 40 to 60 million years ago; about 330 termite species cultivate Termitomyces fungi in their nests.

notes: Mammal, bird and mollusc detail on the page skipped as not soil-related.

definition.text: An organism that gets its energy by oxidizing electron donors from its surroundings, in contrast to phototrophs, which use light.

facts.text: The donors may be organic (chemoorganotrophs) or inorganic (chemolithotrophs), and chemotrophs may be either autotrophic or heterotrophic.

Chemoautotrophs build all their organic compounds from carbon dioxide using energy from substances such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, ferrous iron, hydrogen or ammonia; nitrifiers, methanogens and sulfur oxidizers are among them.
Chemoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon into their own organic compounds; most animals and fungi are chemoheterotrophs.

Methanogens take over the last step of organic matter breakdown only once richer electron acceptors such as oxygen, nitrate and sulfate are used up; thawing frozen soils is expected to raise their methane output.

definition.text: An organism that obtains hydrogen or electrons from organic substrates.

facts.text: The term classifies microorganisms by how they obtain electrons for respiration; Lwoff and collaborators suggested it in 1946.
Many organotrophs, such as animals and many bacteria, are also heterotrophs, and organotrophs can be aerobic or anaerobic.
Its counterpart is the lithotroph, which obtains its electrons from inorganic substrates.

title: Primary nutritional groups

definition.text: The division of organisms by the sources of energy, electrons and carbon they need to live, grow and reproduce.

facts.text: Energy comes from light (phototrophs) or chemical compounds (chemotrophs); electrons from organic donors (organotrophs) or inorganic ones (lithotrophs); carbon from organic compounds (heterotrophs) or carbon dioxide (autotrophs).
Names combine one term from each source: a chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound.
Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used and do not define a nutritional group.
Organotrophs are often also heterotrophs, and lithotrophs are often also autotrophs that use carbon dioxide.
Plants count as lithotrophs because they use water as the electron donor of photosynthesis; cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are photolithoautotrophs.
Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs that take carbon and electrons from dead organic matter; all animals, fungi and protozoa and some bacteria are chemoheterotrophs.
Plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light available.

notes: Bacterial metabolic types (Bacteria#Metabolism) covers the same scheme for bacteria only; this is the general classification page.

title: Microbial metabolism

definition.text: The means by which a microbe obtains the energy and nutrients, such as carbon, that it needs to live and reproduce.

facts.text: A microbe's metabolic properties largely decide its ecological niche and can make it responsible for biogeochemical cycles.
Metabolisms are sorted by carbon source (autotrophic, heterotrophic or mixotrophic), source of reducing equivalents (lithotrophic or organotrophic) and energy source (phototrophic or chemotrophic).
Nitrifying, sulfur-oxidizing and iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs; most bacteria, Bacillus and the Actinomycetota among them, are chemoorganoheterotrophs.
Fermenters use organic carbon instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor; facultative anaerobes respire with oxygen when it is present and switch to fermentation when it is not.
Many facultative anaerobes denitrify because nitrate, like oxygen, has a high reduction potential; nitrate is reduced stepwise through nitrite, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide to dinitrogen.
Methanotrophs oxidize methane step by step to carbon dioxide; because the process needs oxygen, all conventional methanotrophs are obligate aerobes.
Ammonia and nitrite oxidation yield so little energy that nitrifiers grow very slowly; in 2015 the genus Nitrospira was shown to carry out complete nitrification (comammox).

notes: The facultative-anaerobe clause also cites the Facultative anaerobic organism page (S:51742076dfe5), which has no soil content of its own.

definition.text: A size group of small arthropods, usually one to several millimetres long, that live mostly in soil.

facts.text: They include springtails, soil mites such as Oribatida and Mesostigmata, small centipedes, small insects and their larvae, and small crustaceans.
They can move only through existing soil pores and are most common in fallen leaves, litter and the upper soil layers.
They speed the decomposition of organic matter and help form soil structure.
Very sensitive to changes in ecosystems, their communities serve as bioindicators for environmental assessment.

definition.text: Mites are small eight-legged arachnids, and many species live in soil as decomposers.

facts.text: Soil mites span a range of taxa; Oribatida and Prostigmata are more numerous in soil than Mesostigmata and have more soil-dwelling species.
They live in organic debris of all kinds and are extremely numerous in leaf litter.
After a disturbance such as agriculture most mites recolonise soil within a few months, whereas Oribatida take several years.
Most are beneficial, helping decompose organic material as part of the carbon cycle; some Laelapidae are used to control fungus gnats and soil pests.

definition.text: Arthropods of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments.

facts.text: Most are slow-moving detritivores of forest floors that eat decaying leaves and dead wood; some eat fungi or suck plant fluids.
Individual species are estimated to consume 1 to 11 percent of all leaf litter, depending on species and region.
Litter is fragmented in the gut and excreted as pellets of leaf fragments, algae, fungi and bacteria, which helps microbes decompose it further.
Burrowing that mixes organic with mineral matter makes them soil ecosystem engineers, especially where earthworms are absent or scarce, as in some tropical forests.

title: Termites

definition.text: Eusocial insects that eat decaying plant material, mostly wood, leaf litter and soil humus.

facts.text: They are important decomposers in subtropical and tropical regions, and their recycling of wood and plant matter is of considerable ecological importance.
Many species are ecosystem engineers that change soil hydrology, decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth, and so the biodiversity around their large mounds.
Primarily detritivores, they eat dead plants at any stage of decay; higher termites also eat faeces, humus, grass, leaves and roots.
Of 3,014 classified species, 754 live in Africa, where mounds are islands of soil fertility in savannas; the northern Kruger National Park alone has about 1.1 million active mounds.
Nests are subterranean, epigeal (mounds) or arboreal; most termites build underground colonies, using soil for subterranean nests and mounds.
Around 330 species of the Macrotermitinae farm Termitomyces fungi on their faecal pellets in fungus cones inside the nest.
Termite diversity and abundance fall with disturbance, such as loss of trees and soil cover and trampling by cattle and goats.

definition.text: Termite nests that protrude above the soil surface, built of earth and mud and stronger than underground nests.

facts.text: Macrotermes builds some of the largest mounds, 8 to 9 metres high with chimneys, pinnacles and ridges; the largest recorded measured 12.8 metres.
Being rich in clay, mounds in areas of torrential, continuous rain risk erosion.
Compass termites build wedge-shaped mounds aligned north–south, which warms them quickly in the morning but avoids midday overheating.
Mounds shelter birds, lizards, snakes and scorpions, and 54 ant species are known to live in Nasutitermes mounds.

definition.text: Animals adapted to digging that live mainly, though not only, underground.

facts.text: Examples include moles, badgers, naked mole-rats, armadillos and wombats, and among invertebrates many clams, beetles, wasps, bees and spiders.
Small burrowers such as ants, termites and earthworms move so much soil that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift.
Burrowing changes soil composition, structure and vegetation, usually shifting plant species and raising plant diversity.
Mounds and bare soils with burrowers hold more ammonium and nitrate and show greater nitrification potential than vegetated soils, mainly because the grass cover is removed.

definition.text: Carnivorous fungi specialised in trapping and digesting nematodes; more than 700 species are known.

facts.text: They catch prey with adhesive hyphae, knobs or nets, or with hyphal loops that tighten on contact; others stun nematodes with toxins or infect them or their eggs as parasites.
Nematode trappers are concentrated in the upper soil, pastures and leaf litter, mostly in nitrogen-deficient habitats.
Arthrobotrys oligospora builds its costly snares only when it detects nematode pheromones such as ascarosides.
Some are studied for biological control: Purpureocillium lilacinum attacks the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita, though field results have been mixed.

definition.text: A long, branching filament of a fungus, oomycete or actinobacterium; in most fungi hyphae are the main mode of growth and together form a mycelium.

facts.text: A hypha is one or more cells inside a tubular wall, usually of chitin, divided in most fungi by perforated cross-walls called septa.
Hyphae average 4–6 μm across and grow at their tips.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal hyphae alone are estimated to extend about 110 quadrillion kilometres through Earth's topsoils.
Specialised forms include arbuscules that exchange nutrients with plant cells and mycelial cords that move nutrients over long distances.

title: Mycelium

definition.text: The root-like body of a fungus, a mass of branching, thread-like hyphae.

facts.text: Mycelial colonies grow in and on soil, from colonies too small to see to one Armillaria spanning thousands of acres.
It feeds in two stages: hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, which are then absorbed.
Mycelia decompose plant material, add to the organic fraction of soil and release carbon dioxide as they grow.
Mycelial networks make up 20-30% of soil biomass, though traditional biomass measures fail to detect them.
Mycorrhizal mycelium helps most plants take up water and nutrients and by some estimates receives well over 10% of the host's photosynthetic output.
Mycelium is an important food for many soil invertebrates.
Fungi break down lignin in compost, which many other composting microbes cannot.
Fungi can degrade soil contaminants such as petroleum products and some pesticides (mycoremediation), and mycelium spread on logging roads binds disturbed soil.

definition.text: The field between geology and microbiology that studies the role of microbes in geological and geochemical processes and the effects of minerals and metals on microbes.

facts.text: Its interactions take place in rocks, minerals, soils and sediments, the atmosphere and the hydrosphere, where microbes drive biogeochemical cycles, precipitate and dissolve minerals and concentrate metals.
Some bacteria gain energy by reducing dissolved metal ions, and as a side effect concentrate the metals into what can become ore deposits.
In soil, microbes transform mineral and metal speciation, toxicity and mobility, and immobilise and detoxify metals, radionuclides, sulfur and phosphorus.
Cr(VI) is mobile and toxic while Cr(III) is less toxic and precipitates in soils above pH 6, so microbial reduction of Cr(VI) is a low-cost bioremediation technique.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria precipitate metals as sulfides and add bicarbonate alkalinity that neutralises acid mine drainage.
Applications include bioremediation, mining, climate change mitigation and drinking water supply.

definition.text: The study of how microorganisms interact with their environment, also called environmental microbiology.

facts.text: Martinus Beijerinck invented the enrichment culture, and Sergei Winogradsky, studying microbes outside medicine, discovered chemosynthesis.
Lorenz Hiltner recognised the bacteria responsible for denitrification, nitrification and nitrogen fixation.
Microbes drive the nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon cycles, making nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium available in soil.
Microbial relationships include mutualism, commensalism, amensalism and parasitism.

title: Microbial biogeography

definition.text: The study of where microorganisms live, at what abundance and why, across space and time.

facts.text: In 1934 Lourens Baas Becking concluded that 'everything is everywhere, but the environment selects', an idea later challenged by clear geographic patterns in microbial life.
The field grew with cheaper, higher-throughput DNA sequencing that allows global analyses of microbial data.
Unlike most larger organisms, global topsoil microbiomes are more diverse in temperate zones than in the tropics.
Soil bacterial patterns are usually linked to soil pH, which may stand in for the climatic water balance that controls carbon inputs and the connectivity of water-filled habitats.

contested_note: Geographic patterns in microbes dispute the Baas Becking view that microbes are everywhere and only the environment selects.

title: Metagenomics

definition.text: The study of all the genetic material from all organisms in an environment, revealing their composition, diversity and functional potential.

facts.text: It profiles microbial communities without culturing species, and early environmental gene studies showed that cultivation had missed most microbial diversity.
Unlike amplicon sequencing (metabarcoding) of marker genes such as 16S rRNA, which shows which taxa are present, metagenomics sequences all DNA and also recovers enzymes and pathways.
Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991.
One gram of soil holds about 10^9–10^10 microbial cells, about one gigabase of sequence, and soil communities are among the most complex known.
Functional metagenomics explores plant–microbe interactions and the roles of uncultivated or rare community members in nutrient cycling and plant growth.
Because sampling is uncontrolled, the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data.
Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community.
The 16S rRNA gene identifies bacteria and archaea, and 18S rRNA or ITS identifies fungi; more similar sequences are taken to mean closer evolutionary relatedness.

definition.text: A technique that uses the fatty acids of membrane phospholipids as chemical markers to estimate the living microbial biomass and community make-up of soil and water.

facts.text: Phospholipids break down rapidly when organisms die, so the phospholipid content of a sample is taken to come from living cells.
Saponifying the phospholipids releases their fatty acids, whose composition is compared with that of known organisms.
D.C. White pioneered the method in the early to mid 1980s, after a 1965 article proposed using molecules made by organisms as biomarkers.
It became widely used for soil because it measures the dominant microbes sensitively and reproducibly without cultivation, which is costly and biased.
Lipids are extracted from dried soil with a chloroform–methanol–phosphate buffer and the fatty acids analysed as methyl esters by gas chromatography.
The same PLFAs occur in many life forms, including plant roots, fungi and bacteria, so assigning them to specific microbial groups needs care.
Archaeal lipids are ether-linked rather than ester-linked, so routine preparation misses archaea.
Extraction is long and cumbersome, though a 96-well plate procedure raised throughput 4-to-5 fold.

title: PLFA biomarkers of soil microbes
article: Phospholipid-derived fatty acids#The PLFA components of soil microbiota

definition.text: Signature fatty acids in a PLFA profile that indicate particular groups of soil microorganisms.

facts.text: Iso- and anteiso-branched acids such as 15:0 iso estimate Gram-positive bacteria, while acids with a methyl branch at the 10th carbon mark actinomycetes.
Monounsaturated plus cyclopropane acids estimate Gram-negative bacteria, and a high cyclopropane-to-monounsaturated ratio indicates stress.
Linoleic acid, 18:2 ω6c, indicates fungi, and 16:1 ω5c is recommended as a marker for arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
In rice paddy soil, PLFA showed about 44% aerobic bacteria, 32% facultative anaerobes and 24% archaea early on, shifting to 27%, 36% and 37% under longer flooding.

definition.text: A genus of aerobic, free-living soil bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen and release it into the soil as ammonium.

facts.text: They are common in neutral and weakly basic soils but not acid soils, and can survive in dry soil as cysts for up to 24 years.
Unlike Rhizobium they fix nitrogen without a plant partner, and fixation stops when ammonium or nitrate is available.
They shield oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase by speeding up their metabolism; besides the molybdenum-iron enzyme they have a vanadium nitrogenase that fixes nitrogen down to 5 °C.
Martinus Beijerinck described the genus in 1901; Azotobacter is used in nitrogen biofertilizers such as azotobacterin and makes plant hormones such as auxins.

verification.title: Survival of Azotobacter spp. in Dry Soils
verification.evidence: Dry soils stored in glass containers in the laboratory and protected from contamination for periods of 22 to 24 years yielded numerous colonies of Azotobacter chroococcum and other members of the family Azotobacteraceae.
verification.note: the paper recovered Azotobacter from soils stored 22 to 24 years, matching 'up to 24 years'

definition.text: The largest genus of actinomycete bacteria, found mainly in soil and decaying vegetation.

facts.text: Most produce spores and give soil its earthy odour by releasing the volatile compound geosmin.
They are filamentous, Gram-positive bacteria with branched hyphae 0.5–2.0 μm across, forming a substrate mycelium that scavenges organic compounds.
Streptomycetes produce over two-thirds of the clinically useful natural antibiotics; streptomycin is named after the genus.
Several species are plant pathogens, causing scab of potatoes and soft rot of sweet potatoes.

definition.text: Any close and long-term biological interaction between two organisms of different species.

facts.text: Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it in 1879 as 'the living together of unlike organisms'; the word is sometimes kept for mutualism, where both partners benefit.
Symbiosis can be obligate or facultative, and an ectosymbiont lives on its partner while an endosymbiont lives inside its tissues.
Examples include rhizobia in legume root nodules and nitrogen-fixing Frankia in alder root nodules.
Antagonism is shown by black walnut, whose secreted juglone destroys many herbaceous plants within its root zone.

definition.text: The community of microorganisms usually found living together in a given habitat.

facts.text: The term was first defined in 1988 by Whipps and colleagues, who studied rhizosphere microorganisms, as a characteristic community in a well-defined habitat with distinct physico-chemical properties.
Relic DNA can make up to 40% of the DNA sequenced from soil.
Synthetic nitrogen fertiliser may barely change soil microbiome composition but drastically reduces the connectivity of its network.
TerraGenome, a reference soil metagenome project, began in 2008.

title: Detrital food web

definition.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi and passes to detritivores and then carnivores.

facts.text: Detritus is any non-living organic matter: leaf litter, dead wood, carrion, dead microbes and faeces among others.
Most of an ecosystem's primary production is not eaten but recycled through detritus into useful nutrients.
It links to the grazing web: mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that consume decaying leaves.
Basal species of food webs include saprophytic detritivores such as the decomposer community of soil, whose role Raymond Lindeman emphasised.

notes: The rest of the general Food web page has no soil-specific content.

title: Invasive earthworms of North America

definition.text: The spread of introduced, mostly European and Asian earthworms into North American forests, especially northern forests that have lacked native worms since the last ice age.

facts.text: Most northern forests lost their native earthworms to the Wisconsin glaciation, so a deep detritus layer is typical and many native plants rely on it.
Invading worms break up the organic layer by burrowing, eating litter and leaving casts, mixing nutrients beyond the reach of shallow roots, where they may be leached.
Effects include a thinner organic layer, more mineralization, higher bulk density and faster decomposition; podzols lose their banded E horizons.
Invasions reduce plant diversity, seedlings and mycorrhizal associations, while invasive plants such as buckthorn and garlic mustard increase.
European worms arrived in soil with settlers from the 18th century, likely in the root balls of imported plants; recreation, bait and construction now spread them.
Sandy, saline or acidic soils and high C:N litter resist invasion, while high pH and low C:N favour it.
Asian jumping worms of Amynthas and Metaphire grow and breed faster and live at higher densities than European species, stripping the forest floor of organic matter.
Worms cannot be removed from soil, so control aims to slow spread: fewer bait releases, regulated soil movement and heat-treated compost or mulch.

notes: Regional page kept because it documents soil-profile effects (podzol E horizons, bulk density) with global relevance. Its taxa count (182 taxa, 60 introduced; S:68be931d14cd) conflicts with Earthworm#As an invasive species; see Earthworm invasions.

definition.text: Fungi are a kingdom of mostly hypha-forming organisms that, with bacteria, are the major decomposers on land.

facts.text: Most fungi grow as thread-like hyphae 2 to 10 micrometres across and up to several centimetres long, which extend at their tips and branch; their high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants, though they were once classed as plants for their immobile lifestyle.
Along with bacteria they are the major decomposers in most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, so they are central to biogeochemical cycles and food webs.
Over 90% of plant species form mycorrhizal relationships with fungi and depend on them for survival; the symbiosis dates back at least 400 million years.
Lichens pair a fungus with photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria, and some ants cultivate fungi for food and nest structure.
Many fungi are plant parasites, such as the rice blast fungus and those causing Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight.

As of 2019 nine major lineages are recognised, including Chytridiomycota, Glomeromycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota; the last two form the species-rich Dikarya, with all mushrooms and most plant pathogens.

definition.text: Fungi reproduce asexually, sexually or both, and spread mainly by spores.

facts.text: Asexual reproduction uses vegetative spores (conidia) or mycelial fragmentation, in which pieces of mycelium each grow into a separate mycelium.
An estimated third of fungi use more than one method, with a sexual teleomorph stage and an asexual anamorph stage.
Spores of most studied species travel by wind; dry, hydrophobic spores are readily scattered by raindrops.

definition.text: Fungi can protect crops by competing with pathogens or by parasitising them.

facts.text: About 300 species of fungi and fungus-like organisms, in 13 classes and 113 genera, are used as biocontrol agents against plant fungal diseases.
Organisms that parasitise fungi are called mycoparasitic.
Fungi may also compete with pathogenic bacteria or fungi for nutrients and space, by the competitive exclusion principle.

definition.text: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, free-living or parasitic, that feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris.

facts.text: The name is now used loosely for heterotrophic single-celled protists, since Protozoa as a taxon is not monophyletic; classic examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena.
They range from about 1 micrometre to several millimetres, and are flagellates, ciliates or amoebae according to how they move.
All need a moist habitat, but many survive dry spells as resting cysts; they are common in soils and mosses.
All are heterotrophs, engulfing prey by phagocytosis or taking up dissolved matter by osmotrophy, and some are mixotrophs hosting symbiotic algae.
Most reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission; sexual exchange is generally decoupled from reproduction.
In the microbial food web they are the most important bacterivores and mobilise nutrients, passing bacterial and algal production on and solubilising nutrients in microbial biomass.
Termite gut flagellates help their host digest wood by breaking down complex sugars.

title: Organic matter decomposition and humus formation

definition.text: Microbes oxidise soil organic matter partly to carbon dioxide, water and energy, leaving humus, new microbial cells and inorganic plant nutrients.

facts.text: Fresh residues first decompose rapidly, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy and small amounts of inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur.
The microbes' most important function is recycling organic carbon to CO2, which keeps photosynthesis going.
Microbial oxidation turns nutrients from unavailable organic forms into plant-available inorganic ones, so organic matter acts as a slow-release fertilizer that buffers nutrient supply.
Soil with 1% organic matter holds up to 45 million kilocalories per acre-furrow-slice, equivalent to about 6 tons of coal.
Microbes use only a small share of the energy for new cells; making one pound of soil organic matter may destroy 10 to 20 pounds of residues.
Fresh residues accelerate decomposition of humified material already in the soil.
Added organic matter improves tilth and structure, raises cation exchange and water holding capacity and aeration, and reduces erosion.

definition.text: Humus is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of soil organic matter left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes.

facts.text: It has low bulk density (0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre), high porosity and water holding capacity, and a cation exchange capacity above 200 cmol(+) per kilogram.
Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur.
It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates.
Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, with a range from under 1% to over 12%.
Holding the normal humus level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it.
Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year; rotations with grasses and legumes, conservation tillage and residue management help sustain it.

definition.text: Soil organisms are under 0.5% of dry soil mass, and their numbers depend on temperature, moisture, pH, nutrients, energy supply and oxygen.

facts.text: Decay organisms work best at about 20 to 40 degrees C; temperatures outside that range slow most soil organisms.
Too much water cuts the numbers and kinds of organisms through poor aeration, yet at low moisture soil organisms do better than higher plants.
Fungi, bacteria and actinomycetes vary with pH; below pH 6.0 fungi become the dominant microorganisms.
Adding organisms to a soil is usually ineffective because the community is already vast; changing the crop alters populations more.

title: Winogradsky column

definition.text: A simple stratified microbial ecosystem built from sediment in a container, showing different microbial metabolisms.

facts.text: Columns are set up as a control and with added carbon (cellulose), sulfur (egg yolk calcium sulfate) or both, then form oxygen and sulfide gradients.
Purple and green sulfur bacteria use sulfide to support photosynthesis, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple.
He developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context.
It remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world.

definition.text: Some free-living soil bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use to make amino acids and proteins.

facts.text: Plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas or nitrogen locked in organic molecules; it must be converted to ammonium and nitrate, a bacterial process called nitrogen mineralization.
Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living fixers; Azospirillum attaches to root surfaces and makes substances that help plants tolerate stress.
They add only modest nitrogen, but it matters in natural systems where nutrient cycling is efficient.
Rhizobia in legume root nodules receive sugars from the plant and supply usable nitrogen; an alfalfa stand may fix hundreds of pounds per acre a year, peas about 30 to 50.

definition.text: Soil insects such as termites, springtails, ants, fly larvae and beetles are often secondary and tertiary consumers.

facts.text: Springtails eat fungi and animal remains and are prey for predacious mites; many beetles eat other soil animals, and dung beetles bury manure balls.
Millipedes are primary consumers of plant residues, centipedes eat other organisms, mites eat fungi, other mites, insect eggs or residues, and spiders hold insect pests down.
Termites eat wood and also decomposed organic residues in soil.

definition.text: Plant roots influence soil as much as soil influences roots, shaping aggregates and feeding soil organisms.

facts.text: Root pressure brings particles closer, small roots bind them, and root hairs add soil contact for water and nutrient access and help form aggregates.
Roots exude compounds that feed organisms in the surrounding zone; corn sends about 20 percent of photosynthesis sugars to roots early to mid-season.
Mucigel, a sticky layer around roots, gives close contact between microorganisms, soil minerals and the plant.
Roots add organic matter that may decompose more slowly than surface residues; in grasses the living tissue below ground can exceed that above.
Roots do not grow well in compact, nutrient- or water-poor, high-pathogen or extreme-pH soil.

title: Natural suppression of plant pests in soil

definition.text: Diverse soil organisms keep checks and balances that stop disease organisms and parasites from becoming major plant problems.

facts.text: Only a small number of bacteria, fungi, insects and nematodes might harm plants in a given year, and their impact is reduced in more diverse soil.
Some fungi kill nematodes or insects, some produce antibiotics, and protozoa, springtails and mites eat disease-causing fungi and bacteria.
Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens colonize roots and protect them; Bacillus thuringiensis toxin is sold as a biological control agent.
Suppression is thought to arise from competition for nutrients, antagonistic substances or direct parasitism, and some beneficial organisms induce plant immune defenses.

definition.text: Soil organisms span nearly ten orders of magnitude in size, from sub-micrometre bacteria to vertebrates and kilometre-long fungal threads.

facts.text: The smallest soil bacterium is about 0.5 micrometres across, soil-dwelling amphibians and mammals are about 10 cm long, roots run 0.1 to 10 m, and some forest fungi form mycelia of 1 km or more.

Traditional groups are microflora, macroflora (roots), microfauna, mesofauna (0.1 to 2 mm metazoans) and macrofauna (over 2 mm), but the scheme confuses: fungi are called microflora yet are macroscopic and heterotrophic.
A colony of Armillaria ostoyae in an Oregon Douglas fir forest covers several square kilometres and may be the largest organism by area.

Archaea were widely recognized as distinct from bacteria only in the early 1990s; DNA analysis shows them as different from bacteria as from plants or animals, in Woese's three domains Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

definition.text: Sporosarcina pasteurii is a gram-positive, soil-borne bacterium that precipitates calcite and solidifies sand given calcium and urea.

facts.text: It is a rod-shaped endospore former, 0.5 to 1.2 micrometres wide and 1.3 to 4.0 micrometres long, an alkaliphile growing at pH 9 to 10 and surviving up to pH 11.2.
It is a heterotrophic facultative anaerobe needing urea and ammonium, secreting urease to hydrolyse urea for nitrogen, carbon and energy.
Carbonate ions from urea hydrolysis react with calcium to precipitate calcium carbonate that cements sand grains; it is non-pathogenic and makes much urease, so it is a common MICP organism.
It is proposed for self-healing concrete and other bio-cement uses.
